summary: György Hazai worked in linguistics and Iranian and Central Asian studies. He studied at Eötvös Loránd University (~1950–1954) and held a post at the Institut für Orientforschung from circa 1963 to 1982.

A scholar of linguistics and Central Asian studies, Kara studied at Eötvös Loránd University under Gyula Németh and Lajos Ligeti. He held posts at Eötvös Loránd University, the Hungarian Academy of Sciences, and as Professor at Indiana University (1992–2022).
Gyōin Hashimoto was a scholar of Buddhist studies and philosophy who studied under Join Saeki and at the University of Tokyo (~1921–1925). He later served as head (管主) of Yakushiji from 1939 to 1967.
Gé Mang Khenchen Yönten Gyatso studied under Patrul Rinpoche and Jamgon Ju Mipham Gyatso, and he later taught Shechen Gyaltsab.

Working in Indology, religious studies, and history/archaeology, Gérard Colas served as a researcher at the CNRS (attested 2004, 2009) and at the School for Advanced Studies in the Social Sciences (attested 2012).

Gérard Fussman was a scholar of Indology, history/archaeology, and linguistics who studied at the École Normale Supérieure (~1961–1965). Succeeding Jean Filliozat, he served as a professor at the Collège de France beginning in 1984.

Working in Tibetology, Indology, and Central Asian studies, Bethlenfalvy studied at Eötvös Loránd University (1956–1963) under Lajos Ligeti. He held positions at the University of Delhi, Eötvös Loránd University, the Hungarian Academy of Sciences, and the University of Vienna.

Liebert was an Indologist and linguist who earned his doctorate at the University of Gothenburg (~1941–1949). He held positions at Lund University, Uppsala University, and served as professor of comparative linguistics and Sanskrit at Gothenburg (1955–1982).

A historian of Central Asia, von Selle studied at Kiel, Berlin, and Göttingen (Dr. phil. ~1918–1920). He held library posts in Göttingen and Berlin, and was a professor and library director at the University of Königsberg (~1936–1944).
Günter Blamberger worked at the University of Kassel (~1993–1995) and held the Chair in German Philology at the University of Cologne from circa 1995 to 2018.
Günter Grönbold specialized in Indology, Tibetology, and Buddhist studies. He served as Head of the South Asia Department at the Bavarian State Library from circa 1974 to 2008.

Active in Indology and linguistics, Schweiger studied at the Vienna University of Economics and Business under Gert Klingenschmitt. He served as an assistant at Linz (~1966–1972) and as a full professor at WU Vienna (1974–2009).

Melchert is a linguist and Central Asian specialist who completed studies at Michigan State, DLI, NCS, and Harvard. He was a professor at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill (1978–2007) and UCLA (2007–2015).

H. G. Narahari specialized in Indology and linguistics, completing degrees at the University of Mysore and the University of Madras under C. Kunhan Raja. In 1944, he held posts at the Adyar Library and the University of Madras.
H. J. de Graaf was a historian who studied at Leiden University (~1919–1935) and under Poerbatjaraka between 1927 and 1930.

H. V. Nagaraja Rao is a scholar of Indology, philosophy, and linguistics. He has held positions at the Oriental Research Institute Mysore and as a professor at the University of Mysore (attested 2012).
Haeju Sunim works in Buddhist studies. She served as a visiting lecturer at Harvard University (1996–1997) and as an associate professor of Buddhist studies at Dongguk University (attested 1999).

Hu-von Hinüber studied at Peking University under Kemu Jin and Zhongxin Jiang. Active in Indology, Buddhist studies, and Sinology, she held appointments at the University of Vienna (attested 1996) and the University of Freiburg (2010).

A linguist and Tibetologist, Kitamura studied under Tokan Tada at the University of Tokyo. He held posts at NINJAL, Tokyo University of Foreign Studies (1964–1986), Toyo Bunko, and served as president of Reitaku University (attested 1987).

Nakamura studied Indology and Buddhist philosophy at the University of Tokyo under Hakuju Ui, succeeding him in 1943. He taught at Tokyo until 1973, served as a visiting professor at Stanford, and directed the Eastern Institute.
